strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: scaling graph and hypergraph generative models while jointly generating structural topology and continuous node/hyperedge features.

The proposed node budget mechanism is an elegant, localized way to control multi-scale expansion and enforce consistency across varying rates of regional growth, outperforming simple global size conditioning.
Adapting minibatch optimal-transport (OT) coupling to cluster-level child node permutations effectively mitigates permutation noise during training at negligible computational overhead.
Comprehensive technical formulation with detailed algorithms for coarsening, expansion, refinement, training, and sampling in the appendix, along with thorough ablation studies.
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation on featured hypergraphs is quite limited: only 3D coordinates on downsampled meshes (50 vertices, 100 faces) are evaluated as featured hypergraphs, and the only baseline compared against is a simple two-step sequential approach.

Despite motivating hypergraphs strongly with applications in molecular design (rings, scaffolds) and circuit netlists in Section 1 and 2, no experiments on molecular or circuit datasets with rich/discrete attributes are conducted; the paper strictly evaluates 3D coordinates.

Comparison on graph point clouds is against flat models (DiGress, DeFoG) which naturally run out of memory (OOM) at 1024 nodes due to dense all-pairs modeling; comparing against scalable/hierarchical graph baselines adapted for continuous features would provide a more informative benchmark.

The theoretical contributions are modest: Proposition 3/9 (mean minimizes MSE) and Proposition 12 (OT minimizes pairwise distance) are elementary mathematical properties rather than deep structural or probabilistic guarantees.
Empirical runtime, memory consumption, and sampling throughput are not quantitatively reported alongside the quality metrics.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: scaling graph and hypergraph generative modeling while jointly predicting continuous/discrete node and edge features, a setting where existing hierarchical methods (e.g., HYGENE) and flat diffusion models (e.g., DiGress, DeFoG) struggle or run out of memory.

The proposed node budget mechanism is well-motivated and technically sound, effectively handling non-uniform regional expansion during the reverse coarsening process and enforcing node count constraints via simplex projection and inpainting.

The localized adaptation of minibatch optimal transport (OT) coupling is clever and computationally efficient: by restricting permutations to child nodes derived from the same cluster (evaluating only 2 or 6 permutations per parent), it resolves permutation ambiguity without introducing combinatorial overhead.

Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple settings (unfeatured synthetic and real-world hypergraphs, featured 3D meshes, and 1024-node point cloud graphs), supported by thorough ablations and clear visual comparisons.

The paper and supplementary material are well-organized, providing complete algorithms for training and sampling, theoretical derivations, and an asymptotic complexity analysis demonstrating linear scaling $O(n + m + k)$.
weaknesses: Although the framework is formulated for joint node and hyperedge features ($F_L$ and $F_R$), all featured experiments (3D meshes and point clouds) only evaluate continuous 3D coordinate node features, leaving hyperedge feature generation empirically untested.

The featured hypergraph experiments are evaluated only on very small meshes (coarsened to 50 vertices and 100 triangles), and the baseline comparison in that regime is limited to a single sequential two-stage ablation rather than established generative baselines.

Proposition 3 (Proposition 9 in the appendix) is mathematically trivial, as it merely restates the standard property that the arithmetic mean minimizes Euclidean mean squared error; framing it as a notable theoretical result overstates its significance.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated architecture: Extending hierarchical coarsening-expansion graph generation to jointly generate both continuous node features and higher-order topological relations (hypergraphs) addresses a clear open challenge in structured generative modeling.

Effective node budget mechanism: Replacing simple scalar global-size conditioning with localized recursive budget splitting and simplex projections (Von Neumann projection) provides fine-grained control over local expansion rates, directly reducing node count discrepancy (NumDiff) across synthetic and real-world benchmarks.

Efficient permutation alignment via localized OT-coupling: Restricting minibatch optimal transport coupling to the child nodes within each cluster expansion ($K \le 3$) makes the re-indexing computationally inexpensive ($O(1)$ per cluster) while effectively mitigating permutation mismatch and training instability.

Clear presentation and theoretical grounding: The coarsening/refinement formalization is mathematically coherent, and the propositions regarding MSE minimization for feature averaging and marginal preservation under local OT-coupling are sound.
weaknesses: Limited empirical evaluation on featured hypergraphs: While the paper positions itself around joint feature and structure generation, featured hypergraph experiments are restricted to two small classes of Manifold40 coarsened down to only 50 vertices and 100 triangles. This low resolution does not convincingly demonstrate the scalability claim for featured hypergraphs.

Absence of hyperedge feature validation: Although the theoretical formulation and mathematical definitions explicitly include hyperedge features ($F_R$), none of the evaluated datasets actually include hyperedge features (only 3D spatial coordinates on nodes are used). The hyperedge feature capability remains unvalidated.

Mismatch between motivated applications and experimental scope: The introduction strongly motivates the need for hypergraph generation in molecular design (rings, scaffolds) and electronic circuits with categorical attributes. However, the current framework is restricted to continuous coordinates, omitting standard molecular benchmarks (e.g., QM9, ZINC) and categorical feature handling.

Missing relevant domain baselines: For 3D meshes, the only baseline is an internal sequential ablation (generating topology first, then features). No comparisons are provided against established mesh generative models (e.g., PolyGen, MeshGPT). Similarly, for point cloud graphs, flat baselines (DiGress, DeFoG) fail due to OOM at $N=1024$, but standard scalable 3D generative baselines are not included.

Qualitative generation quality: As shown in the visual samples in Appendix I, the generated 3D meshes are highly irregular and low-poly, and the generated point clouds display noticeable noise and structural artifacts compared to ground-truth geometries.

strengths: Joint hierarchical generation of topology and features: While prior hierarchical graph/hypergraph models (e.g., HSpectre, HYGENE) only handled unfeatured structures, FAHNES presents a unified framework capable of jointly generating topology and continuous features for both standard graphs and hypergraphs.

Scalability and efficiency: The coarsening-expansion approach with local PPGN achieves quasi-linear complexity $O((n+m+k)\log n)$, allowing the model to scale to graphs with ~1000 nodes (such as point cloud graphs) where flat diffusion models like DiGress and DeFoG fail with out-of-memory errors.

Well-motivated technical components: The hierarchical scale encoding effectively guides local expansion budgets across non-uniformly coarsened regions. The local multi-scale OT coupling directly resolves permutation ambiguity among child nodes in an efficient ($O(1)$ per cluster) manner, backed by theoretical propositions.

Extensive empirical validation: The framework is rigorously evaluated across diverse benchmarks—unfeatured hypergraphs, standard unfeatured graphs, 3D meshes represented as hypergraphs, and graph point clouds—demonstrating substantial improvements over existing hierarchical methods and sequential feature-generation baselines.
weaknesses: Limitation in feature types and datasets: The featured experiments are restricted to 3D spatial coordinates (mesh vertices and point clouds). The framework is not tested on discrete/categorical attributes or heterogeneous feature spaces common in molecular or biochemical networks.

Lack of hyperedge features in benchmark evaluation: While the theoretical formulation and bipartite architecture accommodate hyperedge features, none of the experimental datasets contain true hyperedge features.

Modest mesh resolution: The 3D mesh experiments are conducted on simplified low-poly meshes (50 vertices, 100 triangles) and relatively small dataset splits (e.g., 144 training samples for Bench), which limits the demonstration of generating high-resolution mesh topologies.

Mixed benefit of OT coupling on certain topological metrics: As shown in the ablation studies (Tables 5 and 10), while the multi-scale graph OT coupling markedly benefits feature generation metrics like ChamDist, its impact on topological metrics for unfeatured hypergraphs (such as spectral MMD) is somewhat marginal or mixed.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: scalable generative modeling of both topology and features for graphs and hypergraphs, where prior hierarchical methods only handled unfeatured structures and flat diffusion models suffer from quadratic complexity.

Technically well-grounded framework introducing several synergistic components: (1) hierarchical scale encoding to track remaining expansions and enforce node budgets across heterogeneous growth rates, (2) local multi-scale OT coupling to resolve permutation ambiguity within expanded clusters with minimal (~4%) computational overhead, and (3) active-node loss masking (graph inpainting) to prevent gradient dilution from trivial identity mappings at finer scales.

Theoretical support is provided for key design choices, including optimal feature coarsening (Proposition 1), unbiased marginals and variance reduction for multi-scale OT coupling (Propositions 2 and 3), and gradient signal preservation under node masking (Proposition 4).

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple domains, including unfeatured hypergraphs, unfeatured standard graphs, 3D mesh hypergraphs, and 1000-node point cloud graphs where standard flat diffusion baselines (DiGress, DeFoG) run out of memory.
Well-written manuscript accompanied by comprehensive supplementary material containing explicit pseudocode algorithms, complexity proofs, detailed ablation studies, and qualitative visualizations.
weaknesses: Limited variety in feature modalities: The experiments with features are strictly restricted to 3D geometric coordinates (continuous Euclidean features in meshes and point clouds). The paper does not evaluate standard graph benchmarks with categorical node/edge features (e.g., molecular graphs such as QM9 or ZINC).

The 3D mesh experiments are conducted on heavily simplified meshes (50 vertices, 100 triangles), which does not fully demonstrate the scalability benefits of hypergraph generation on complex geometric shapes.

Mesh baselines are somewhat basic: The method is compared primarily against simple flattened image-grid concatenations (WGAN, VAE, Flow Matching) and a sequential two-stage model, rather than specialized geometric mesh generative architectures like MeshGPT or PolyGen (though the conceptual differences are acknowledged in related work).

Ablation results in Table 5 indicate that the multi-scale OT coupling yields somewhat mixed empirical benefits across datasets (e.g., minor or negligible differences on ModelNet Bookshelf/Piano and ManifoldNet Bench), suggesting its utility may depend heavily on data characteristics.

strengths: Principled generalization of hierarchical generative modeling: The paper successfully extends the coarsening-expansion paradigm (previously restricted to unfeatured structures) to jointly generate topology and continuous node/hyperedge features within a flow-matching framework.

Scalability: By utilizing a localized hierarchical expansion mechanism on the bipartite incidence representation, the model achieves quasi-linear complexity O((n + m + k) log n), successfully training and sampling on 1000-node graph point clouds where flat diffusion baselines (DiGress, DeFoG) run out of memory.

Well-designed technical components: The hierarchical scale encoding provides a neat mechanism to enforce local node budget conservation, and the local multi-scale OT coupling is computationally lightweight due to small cluster sizes (evaluating only 2 to 6 permutations).
Thorough ablation studies: The experiments systematically evaluate the impact of scale encodings, graph OT coupling, and coarsening strategies (spectral vs. feature-preserving vs. random).
weaknesses: Restricted feature modality: Despite the broad framing of 'feature-aware' graph and hypergraph generation, the experiments and methodology are exclusively evaluated on continuous 3D spatial coordinates. The framework lacks support for mixed categorical/discrete attributes (e.g., atom and bond types), avoiding standard molecular graph generation benchmarks (e.g., QM9, ZINC) which represent the primary benchmark for featured graph generation.

Very low mesh resolution and crude visual fidelity: For 3D mesh hypergraph generation, the evaluation is limited to drastically downsampled low-poly meshes of only 50 vertices and 100 triangles. Even at this low resolution, the generated meshes in Appendix J exhibit notable geometric artifacts, irregularities, and self-intersections.

Overstated theoretical contributions: Several propositions presented as theoretical foundations are either standard results or straightforward reformulations. Proposition 1 simply states that the sample mean minimizes Euclidean variance; Proposition 2 and 3 are standard minibatch OT properties; Proposition 4 is an intuitive motivation regarding loss masking for stationary nodes presented as a formal proposition.

Missing comparisons with specialized mesh and point cloud generative models: While the paper frames 3D shapes as a primary application of hypergraphs, the baselines are limited to generic image-space formulations and standard flat graph models. A comparison or discussion against standard mesh/point-cloud generative baselines (e.g., PointFlow, PolyGen, MeshGPT) is missing to establish practical competitiveness.

High variance across evaluation metrics: For several datasets (e.g., ModelNet Piano in Table 1 and Table 6), the standard deviations across runs for node counts and spectral metrics are remarkably large (e.g., Harmonic distance 119.158 ± 81.023), indicating potential generation instability.
